utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning, Madam Registrar. Could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case IT-05-88-T, The Prosecutor versus Vujadin Popovic, et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. All the accused are here today. Prosecution is Mr. McCloskey, Mr. Thayer, Mr. Mitchell. Defence teams are in full force today like yesterday. We have heard there are some preliminaries who wishes to go first, Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Good morning judges all colleagues in the court room very quickly this morning, Mr. President, I would like to come back to the transcript of yesterday at page 27156 at lines 18 to 23.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One minute. I didn't know what you were going to refer us to, so I don't have in front of me yesterday's.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: It's only one sentence, Mr. President, that I will read out and make a very short preliminary statement. Mr. President, yesterday, a ruling on a Defence objection the Trial Chamber stated that there is no legal basis which would entitle us to restrict the Prosecution from making use of documents which are not on the 65 ter list if the need for such document arises out of the examination-in-chief or the testimony of the witness. For the record, Mr. President, I would like to state that we respectfully disagree with the Trial Chamber's ruling and that we will be filing a motion next week on this issue because we believe that the Prosecution's use of new documents renders these proceedings unfair, in addition to the fact that it is unnecessarily extending the duration of the proceedings. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Do what you like. And for the future, please, we don't need advance notice of this taking precious two or three minutes of our time. So you can proceed with filing what you wish to file without letting us know. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: We join, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Ms. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: The Popovic defence also sports this request made by our colleague Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, any other preliminaries? So let's bring in the -- first we deal with the documents. Borovcanin documents. Mr. Lazarevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning, everyone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: We tendered a list of documents that we used through this witness and we would like them to be admitted into evidence. It's a total of 26 documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Any objections from the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, and as for document -- I apologise. I need to make one further clarification. As for documents 4D605, it's a voluminous document. We ask only two page toss be admitted. Two pages which were used during examination of this witness in order to -- which are translated into English and these this is document which was used to identify the handwriting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But in the list, does it show that particular part of it? Because I don't think --

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, the English does reflect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah. But the B/C/S doesn't. The English says 1682 to 1681.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: We will correct that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Okay. Any objection, Mr. Thayer?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Morning, Mr. President. No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Any objection from the other Defence teams? No objection. They are also admitted. They have been translated, haven't they, Mr. Lazarevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Madam Fauveau, you have two documents?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. 5D1385 and 5D95 and 96.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: 5D95 and 96.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, any objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Any objection from the other Defence teams? None. They are so admitted.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just to correct the transcript, actually, I think I made a mistake. It's 5D13, 85 and 86.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, madam. So we come to the Prosecution exhibits.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, we did distribute a list last night. The first item on the list has been listed in error, we are not intending to offer this statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. Which? Can you give me the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. You are not offering that?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Any objections? None from Mr. Lazarevic. Any objections from the other Defence teams? None. Have they all been -- most of them are in B/C/S. Will we require --

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I think, Mr. President, there may be two documents that were not translated. 3817, one of the documents concerning the PTT lines. The -- I'll have to check with respect to the materiel lists because there were unofficial translations from the prior case that were available, so I'll double-check on those, but I think we -- I think we had them. If not, we'll take care of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We didn't see them when it was shown.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I apologise, Your Honour. I thought that they had been uploaded because they were available for the prior case. Okay. We'll go ahead and take care of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. So they are all admitted with the proviso that those which are not yet translated will be MFI'd pending translation thereof. Any other preliminaries or anything else you would like to ask before we bring in the witness? Why don't we dispose of the two ... Let's start with the last one in time. The Miletic Defence team on the 20th of October filed a motion seeking authorisation to add to the 65 ter list of exhibits 65 documents which were identified in the material provided after the original -- in material provided after the original 65 ter list of exhibits. We would like to know if the Prosecution has already taken a position on this because although the Miletic case was not probable to start soon. Yes, Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, we have not taken a look at the motion yet. However, I anticipate not having objections. We typically have not had a single objection to these motions to add documents or witnesses to the 65 ter list, but we'll get back to you as soon as we have a chance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. So, Mr. Lazarevic, you will recall your filing of the 17th of October, giving notice and also making a submission in relation to be exhibits from the testimony of Krsto Simic under rule 92 bis, and that notice rather, you had stated that you were attaching all of the exhibits used during the testimony of Krsto Simic in the other case, in the Blagojevic case. Following your motion of the 24th of September for the admission pursuant to rule 92 bis of the evidence of Krsto Simic and another person, and the Prosecution response of the 3rd of October 2008, we decided on the 10th of October to admit the transcript of the testimony of Krsto Simic pursuant to the rule of 92 bis subject to the condition that the Defence team for Borovcanin provided the exhibits referred to in it. Now, the above notice has been checked and it does contain all the exhibits in referred to in the Simic transcript. Accordingly, the transcript can be admitted pursuant to rule 92 bis, and we are deciding accordingly. All right. So and you needed to know that of course, in a timely fashion. The last thing, Mr. Lazarevic, again you will recall your motion concerning admission of notability report under Rule 94 bis which you filed on the 13th of October 2008, in that motion you sought leave to amend the 65 ter exhibit list. That was to include a report and audibility of certain communication devices. Secondly to -- you sought the exercise of the discretion on our part to set a reasonable time limit within which the Prosecution should indicate its position on the need for cross-examination of the authors of the report, and in addition, of both authors to the report, the addition of both authors to the report to the 65 ter list with a view to one or both of them being called to offer testimony. In its report which was filed on the 16th of October, the Prosecution stated that it did not object to the addition of the report, and its authors to the 65 ter list, but it does give notice pursuant to Rule 94, that it wishes to cross-examine the authors. Both authors, as I understand it. Since the report -- we have basically concluded that since the report was disclosed on the 3rd of October 2008 by the Borovcanin Defence team, the notice by the Prosecution pursuant to rule 94 bis paragraph(b) was made within the 30 day period required therein. Therefore, the your request to set a reasonable time within which the Prosecution should indicate its position is now moot and will not be deciding on it. Having premised all this, we are deciding as follows: We are granting the request of the Borovcanin Defence team to amend its Rule 65 ter list Exhibit list so as to include the report on audibility of certain communication devices next to it and to add both authors of the report to the 65 ter witness list. And lastly, we are acknowledging the notice of the Prosecution pursuant to Rule 94 bis that it wishes to cross-examine the authors of the report, and therefore you will have that opportunity, if you still wish to cross-examine those two witnesses when the time comes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I can just add, Mr. President, that we've agreed that only one of the authors needs to be available for cross. Mr. Markovic, so we've cut that by a witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, we had a communication with the OTP, and that's what we agreed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. But at least we have cleared this from our table. We can bring in the next witness, Mr. Simic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This is a 92 ter witness, you are aware of that? Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Simic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Before you start your testimony as a Defence witness for accused Borovcanin, you need to make a solemn declaration that you will be testifying the truth. Madam Usher is going to give you the text of the declaration, please read that aloud and that will be your solemn declaration with us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, sir. Please make yourself comfortable. We'll do our utmost to finish your testimony today. Mr. Gosnell is going to go first. He will then be followed by others. Mr. Gosnell.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President, good morning, Your Honours. Good morning, everyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Simic.

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: As I'm sure you recall my name is Chris Gosnell, and I'll be asking you a few questions this morning on behalf of Mr. Borovcanin. Would you please state your full name and date of birth for the record, please.

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: Ljubisav Simic. 8th of August 1953.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And, sir, have you previously testified before the Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes, four years ago, I think. I think almost four years ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: In which case was that?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: The Blagojevic case.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And over the last several days, have you had the opportunity to listen to audio recordings of your testimony?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And, sir, does the audio recording accurately reflect what you said during your testimony in the Blagojevic case?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes, completely.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And if you were asked the same questions again that you were asked during your testimony in the Blagojevic case, would you give the same answers?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat his answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Simic, the interpreters didn't catch your answer. If you could repeat it, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I would repeat the same answers to the same questions that I gave four years ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Mr. President, on the basis of those answers, we tender Mr. Simic's testimony in the Blagojevic case as an exhibit in this case, and we already have a number, 4D606.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Any objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Not at this time. However, should we go over the complete testimony again, I may object, but if it's -- if we don't, I won't be having any objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Mr. President, I should also mention that in going through the transcript with Mr. Simic, we discovered that there were some discrepancies between the audio recording, and we've spoke within the Prosecution about this and we propose to deal with it by consent or agreement. Since, of course, the witness does not speak English and is not in a position to make any comment about --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead, you speak the same language, so please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: All right. Thanks, Mr. President. If it pleases, the court Mr. President, I'd now like to read a summary of the witness's testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Mr. Simic, I'm now going to read a summary of your testimony. Just to make sure you understand, your testimony is now before the Court, that is your evidence and this is purely a summary for the information of others who may not be so interested. Do you understand that?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: "Ljubisav Simic testified in the Blagojevic and Jokic trial on 15 April 2004. Mr. Simic was the president of the municipal assembly of Bratunac in July 1995. He participated in an informal meeting on 12 July 1995. " One short correction, Mr. President, I understand that it appears on the transcript as "meetings" was translated as "meetings," I am sorry, in the B/C/S. So just to repeat: "Mr. Simic participated in an informal meeting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Singular.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Yes, singular. "... on 12 July 1995 at about 8.00 a.m. with General Mladic and others in the Bratunac Brigade headquarters where he was told about the large number of refugees who had gathered at the UNPROFOR compound in Potocari. He was told that he would need to respond to the humanitarian needs of these civilians by providing water, food, and medical facilities. He participated in a second meeting at around 10.00 a.m. at the Hotel Fontana, attended by, amongst others, General Mladic, UNPROFOR officers, a MUP representative, and representatives of the Bosnian-Muslim civilian population. Mr. Simic arranged for water tanks to be sent to Potocari for the civilians, and gave instructions to the Bratunac health clinic to be ready to provide medical assistance. He also went to Ljubovija, a town in Serbia, just on the other side of the Drina river to obtain food. He negotiated with officials at the border to assure the delivery of this food to Potocari. He also called the UNHCR in Belgrade and requested their assistance. Mr. Simic personally went to Potocari that day and saw the civilians outside the DutchBat compound. While there, Mr. Simic observed that the civilians were racing to get on to the buses, and that the Serb and DutchBat soldiers there had to hold them back to prevent a stampede. Mr. Simic spent a time there personally assisting the refugees who were provided with water and bread. He was also escorted inside the DutchBat compound by a Dutch officer. A convoy of trucks from the UNHCR arrived in Bratunac on the evening of 12 July, and the supplies were handed over to the Red Cross for distribution. The evacuation of civilians from Potocari continued on the 13th of July and was completed that day. Mr. Simic heard on the 14th of July that Muslim prisoners had been killed at the Kravica warehouse the previous day. He heard that the killings had started with the killing of a Serb policeman. Mr. Simic spoke with Miroslav Deronjic who was also informed about this event, and who was as shocked as he was at the news. Mr. Simic also testified about his contacts with General Morillon and about an evacuation of civilians that General Morillon organised and led in 1993." Your Honours, that concludes the summary of Mr. Simic's testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Now, sir, I have a few additional questions now to ask you. In your testimony you say that you attended the meeting at the Hotel Fontana starting at around 10.00 a.m., and you've given a description of what happened at that meeting at pages 7608 to 7609 of the transcript, amongst other page references. Now, sir, I don't wish you to recapitulate what happened at the meeting, I simply wish to ask you, do you recall approximately how long the meeting lasted?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: That meeting could have lasted not more than one hour, even if you take into account what happened later, some kind of informal talks that we were held in that other part of the hotel where the meeting was held.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And what is the first thing that you did after the meeting had ended?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: The first thing that I did after the meeting once we started working on the implementation of the things that we had agreed when we realised what we had to do, I divided up the tasks with the -- with Srbislav Davidovic the president of the executive board so that the two of us could deal with what was on our plate, and to see how we could do it in the most economic manner possible so that he could go to the civilian protection and provide tanks with drinking water to dispatch them to Potocari, to go up there and together with the people who were at the meeting to see what needed to be done. And I myself was to organise the healthcare centre to -- and also to collect as much food as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: All right, sir. And what did you do, you said that you spoke to Mr. Davidovic, what did you do after you had finished speaking with Mr. Davidovic?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: Well, we parted ways at one point. I said that I would go to the healthcare centre to tell them that they should urgently set up things there in order to be able to receive indefinite number of the wounded and the sick people who had been hospitalized by the Dutch battalion, where probably the conditions didn't exist for that because it was a factory. And they were probably out in the open air or in tents. So I told them that they should mobilise all of their staff and to rearrange the premises there to put beds in so that people could receive treatment. I also said that all the medical staff from the healthcare centre should be invited in to work because of the emergency situation so that everything could function there. I went on from there to Ljubovija where I wanted to get some food because at that time in Bratunac a very small number of shops was open, and we couldn't provide enough food.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Now, sir, I understand from your testimony in Blagojevic that you weren't wearing a watch, and you expressed considerable uncertainty about precise times, but I would simply like to ask you your best recollection, in general terms, as to when you may have arrived in Ljubovija, even by making reference to a time of day, if not an exact time.

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: Not only at that time. I, in general, don't have a watch. I explained that. I have some personal reasons for this. So after the meeting which ended, well, let us say that I left Fontana at 11, I went to the medical care centre to Ljubovija, it may have been around 12, around 12, so I was in Ljubovija let's say at 12 at the municipality because I went there to ask the colleague from the neighbouring municipality to he could get the people from Ljubovija to give us as much food as possible, bread, milk, food that is ready to eat, that doesn't need to be cooked. And for those people to bring this food to Potocari. I explained to him who this food was for. I may have stayed there about half an hour, not longer, because I couldn't go into the office and ask for all that right from the door. I sat down, we had coffee, we talked a little bit about why I was there, and he immediately started making phone calls while I was still there. He was probably talking to some privately owned bakeries and shops, whatever he could, and he promised that he would do that. I asked him that once this was done, that the people should bring all that to Potocari, and I said that I would head out. I think that from there, in fact, I called the UNHCR --

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Sir, may I just, well, I'm sorry for interrupting, and, in fact, you were about to mention that you called the UNHCR. Perhaps you can tell us precisely about that telephone call.

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: Well, the UNHCR had its office in Belgrade, and I had been in contact quite often with them. I would meet with them because they provided food not only to Bratunac but the whole area. And I thought that their assistance, given that Ljubovija was such a small place that their assistance might be of great importance, perhaps crucial importance, and that's why I called them and told them that perhaps they could intervene, providing as much food as possible, ready-to-eat food, because this food was meant for the people who had spent a night in Potocari in open air and they needed food after all that time because they needed food after spending the whole day and perhaps there would be other days that would follow, so they promised that they would do all they could.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yeah, this is almost all repetition from what is in the trial transcript, I don't wish to have to cross-examine on this material again, so if I could just make that comment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Gosnell, if we could avoid repetition. I know it's mostly not your fault. It's the witness's fault, but if you could draw the attention to the witness. He needs to avoid repeating what he has told.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I will attempt to instruct him.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Thank you for your answer, Mr. Simic, but now I want just to focus on the sequence of events. From Ljubovija where did you go next? Without going into extensive detail about what you did along the way and so forth, if you could simply tell us where you went after Ljubovija.

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: I went to the customs office, and I did what I had to do in order to be able to cross and then I went to the healthcare centre because it was on my way there, I didn't want to have to go back, and then I proceeded to Potocari.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Sir, when you were at the border station, do you recall making any, or having any conversations at the border station? If you could briefly tell us what conversation you might have had?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: At the border crossing I talked to the international observers who were there because there were sanctions imposed on the Republika Srpska and I talked to them. In fact, I asked them, I told them that some people with some food should come in my wake. I told them that this was not stuff to be sold, this was meant for the people from Potocari. I didn't have any paperwork. I said I did not intend to sell this, they did not intend to sell this. I tried to convince them that really this was for the people from Potocari, and I asked them to give approval for this food to go across the border, and I said this would go to Potocari. And they, in fact, gave me their assurances that they would allow this food to pass, and that's what they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Thank you very much, sir. Now, you've just told us that you went from Ljubovija to the border crossing and then from the border crossing to the Bratunac health centre. Where did you go after the Bratunac health centre? Again without describing in great detail what you may have done along the way.

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: From the healthcare centre I went straight to Potocari.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And, sir, you have described what you saw at Potocari in general terms.

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: So I simply want to lead you through the sequence, and then I'm going to ask you a couple of specific questions. You remember testifying in Blagojevic that at some point after you had arrived in Potocari, you got into a car with General Mladic and drove to Srebrenica town. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Can you tell us how long it was between the time that you first arrived in Potocari and the time that you got into the car with General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: I may have come to Potocari between 1300 and 1330 hours, and I think at around 1600 hours, the general came by in a car, he picked me up, and we went to Srebrenica. So it may have been around 1400 hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Okay. And you've described various observations that you made at -- well, strike that question, Your Honour. How long did you spend with General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: Well, I think it may have been around one hour.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And how did you come to leave General Mladic's company?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: Well, this crowd that came together so suddenly dispersed just as suddenly. I left on the way from Srebrenica in Potocari, I went out, because that's where I had parked my car, and he just went on to Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: So do I understand then that he left you in Potocari, or where did he leave you precisely?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes. In Potocari, almost at the same spot where I got into the car, that's where I left the car on our way back from Srebrenica, and he just proceeded towards the town.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And how long did you then spend at Potocari after General Mladic had dropped you off?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: I stayed there for a short time because I could see that there had been no major changes. I was already hungry, tired, and dirty, and I decided to go home to have lunch, to get some rest, and I decided that I would await in my home to see what would happen with the UNHCR convoy because I knew that it was out of my hands now. I couldn't do anything about the time of their arrival, whether it would be earlier or later, so I had no influence over that anymore. So when I went home, I waited there, I thought that they would call me --

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: May I just stop you there, and ask you one question. You describe observing various things at Potocari in your Blagojevic testimony, the distribution of water and food and other assistance that was provided. And you testified about people running towards buses and a stampede. I simply wish to ask you, were those things that you observed during your first interval of time in Potocari, or were they on the second period of time that you were in Potocari?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: I saw those things when I went back from Ljubovija, that was the first time that I was in Potocari. It may have been between 1300 and 1330 hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: So do you confirm then that you saw water being distributed during the first interval of time when you first arrived at Potocari?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes, I parked the car further down from the point where the buses were making the turn because there was not enough place up there. I thought that it would be in their way. So I went down there to park it, and when I went back up I saw that the tank truck was parked to the right-hand side of the road to Srebrenica where the people were gathered, a large crowd, and they were approaching the tank truck and getting the water from there, from that mass of people who were awaiting evacuation. I met the president of the executive board, I asked him if everything was okay, he says yes, as far as we were concerned. He asked me what I had done, and then I asked him about the others, where they were. I meant the people from the meeting. He said no one has shown up yet and he was waiting there for them. He says, "well, there's nothing left for me to do," and so he left.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. I'd like now to move away from Potocari to a new topic and ask you for a few clarifications concerning how you learned about the killings at Kravica warehouse. Now, you said during your Blagojevic testimony that you heard -- you were told about the killings the day after they had occurred. If you recall, who was it who informed you of this?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: The director of the farming co-op, Zoran Nikolic. It was in the morning I think, after that event, came to see us in that office, and he asked us whether we knew what had happened in Kravica. He asked me and the president of the executive board because we were sitting down and having coffee at that time. He told us that this thing that I described had happened there. We asked him if he knew who had done that. He said that he didn't know anyone, but he told us what he had heard, and this is what I said in my previous testimony. If you need me to repeat it, then I will, but if I don't have to repeat it, you have it on record.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: No, sir, I don't need you to repeat it, and thank you for that discretion. Now, when you said who it was to told you, I want to confirm the first name of that person. Would you please tell us again the first name of that person.

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: Jovan Nikolic was the director of the Kravica farming co-op.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And as best as you can recall, can you remember Mr. Nikolic's precise words when he spoke to you?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: He said something horrible happened up there, and then I don't know whether he heard it or he saw it when he went there, I'm not quite sure about that, but I think you have his testimony about that, and he is in a better position to tell you all that. He said that he had heard that a police officer had been killed up there, and that after that murder, people who were there, who had been brought there from somewhere were fired at and that they were killed. And when I asked who did this foolish thing, whether he knew what unit did it, he said that he couldn't recognise anyone and that he tried to approach them to go into the building but they treated him quite roughly and refused entrance. So he couldn't do anything else there. So that would be it, in short, what I can recall. We were quite taken aback by what had happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Sir, I'd like to now just conclude with two very brief topics, and the first topic is to rewind to the meeting at the Hotel Fontana at 10.00 a.m. You've testified that there was a gentleman from the MUP named Mr. Vasic at that meeting. Was there anyone else from the MUP present at that meeting, as best you can recall?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: I recall quite clearly that there was nobody else from the MUP there. There was just him.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. And my last topic is to ask you, sir, whether you saw Mr. Borovcanin in July 1995?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: I saw Mr. Borovcanin only on TV, and from the TV footage, I was able to realise that he had been there, but I personally had not seen him.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Do you recall when it was that you saw this on television, approximately?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: Well, after the evacuation from Srebrenica, B92 TV, I think so, well, I saw them. There may have been others who showed this footage, the arrival of General Mladic and his address and the arrival of Ljubomir Borovcanin and I think he was accompanied by two or three other men, that's what I saw. And that's when I realised that he had been there when Mladic had the first contact with the people who had gathered there in Potocari. I did not meet with him. I did not see him at all on that day. I, in fact, didn't know that he was in town at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And, sir, in July 1995, how was it that you knew who Mr. Borovcanin was?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: Well, we knew Mr. Borovcanin from before, because I think that in late 1992 he came to Bratunac and he was the commander of the police station.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: One moment, Mr. President, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: No further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PROST
utterances.text: Mr. Gosnell, sorry. Just before you sit down, I just want the to a clarify the first points you made about the corrections to the transcript, I take it those will be filed with the Chamber, is that the case?

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I believe that we will perhaps refer it back to CLSS, if necessary, and then we will make a filing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PROST
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you Judge Prost. Thank you Mr. Gosnell. Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. No question for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Ostojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: If I could get the podium.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: My name is John Ostojic, I represent Ljubisa Beara in this case. I'm going to be asking you some questions in connection with some of the things you said in your statement in Blagojevic on the 15th of April 2004. Thank you. First of all, before I do that, sir, I'd like to know if you knew and individual by the name of Miroslav Deronjic.

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And how long had you known him during the period of 1992 through 1995?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: We are school friends since elementary school and we knew each other, we are from Bratunac, we completed the same university but he completed his in Sarajevo, I completed my in Belgrade. We also socialized after we returned to Bratunac. I worked in Bratunac and he worked in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. And would you describe your relationship as being close?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: We were close. Bratunac has few people whom I could socialize with, like I could hang out with him. I mean, we have the same profession, we have lots of common topics to talk about.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And would the same hold true also for Mr. Davidovic?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: I knew Mr. Davidovic as a citizen in Bratunac and somebody who was known to everybody as a good man. I knew him briefly while he was doing something in the police force, but I got to know him better when he became the president of the executive board at the assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. And you dealt with him quite often actually in July 1995 when he was president of the executive board, did you not?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And one last question with an individual, how about Dragan Mrkovic, can you tell me what your relationship was with him in 1995?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: He is also a citizen of ours. I knew him from before the war. I don't know if he held any particular post, but he worked at the town utility company.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. Well, do you have or maintain any relationship or contact with him presently?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: I don't see him so frequently now because he works somewhere else. I don't know exactly what he -- his job is, but I heard that he spends most of his time in Montenegro working in the construction business, that's his profession. And this is how he supports himself now, in construction. I don't see him that often.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. Well, in 1995 July, did you hear of whether he had any involvement at all with the burial of Bosnian-Muslims from the Kravica warehouse to the area known as Glogova? Were you familiar with that at all?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: I didn't know anything about that or talked about that later. At that point in time, I didn't know anything about it. The person who is supposed to know about it is the president of the executive board. If he knew it, then he knew it, but I don't know if he knew it or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: That would be Davidovic; right?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And do you know if Mrkovic was also a member of the SDS in July of 1995?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes, I think that he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And you were as well; correct?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And Mr. Davidovic was?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: I'm not sure about him. Perhaps he joined later, but I think that he -- that I actually proposed him as a member of the executive board to Mr. Deronjic because I wanted to leave my own post unless he was appointed president of the executive board I was intending to resign.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. And Mr. Deronjic was obviously the president of the SDS during that time, 1992 through 1995 at the very least; correct?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes, and president of the deputy's club of the SDS.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you for that. Let me ask you specifically with respect to July of 1995, we heard and read your testimony in connection with your travels and your visit to Potocari, but we need to be, if we can at all, be a little more precise with the time in which you claimed you met some people. So it is my understanding that on the 12th of July 1995, you actually went to Potocari, or was that the 13th of July 1995?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: On the day of the evacuation, I said that in my previous testimony. Not only then, but it's actually my trait, I don't actually remember dates, but it was on the day of the evacuation, whether that was on the 12th or the --

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. Let's try it this way then: The day you had the meeting at the Hotel Fontana I think it was recorded, and I believe that's no dispute about that, was the 12th of July 1995 at 10.00 that you mentioned. If we just accept that as being true, then did you go to Potocari that same day or the next day?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: That same day because after the meeting we proceeded to Potocari.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: And that's when -- to carry out the evacuation.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, what did you do on the 13th of July, that is the day after you were at the Potocari and the day after the Hotel Fontana? Describe for me what you did that day?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: I came later, not that much later but I was actually late for work that morning, I came straight to the office to the president of the executive board to chat because I hadn't seen him from the day before, to see what was new. So I dropped by at the municipal office.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: Do I need to say anything else?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Not right now, thank you. On the 13th of July 1995, did you have any meetings with Mr. Deronjic?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: No, I did not see Mr. Deronjic that day. I heard a little bit before, and I conveyed to Mr. Davidovic that he was supposed to find Mr. Deronjic, I was not able to see Deronjic. I saw him when he came from Potocari and brought some paper containing some stamps that the evacuation had been completed and the commander of the Dutch battalion, I think, had signed another man who had attended the meeting and Deronjic and he brought that on paper to the municipal office and said this should be archived because it was a document that had to be kept.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: So as far as you are concerned, the evacuation was completed on the evening of the 12th of July 1995; correct?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: I stopped going up there at all because I saw that there was no point in doing that because everything that was expected of me I had done and then it was up to the Red Cross after that, and I didn't see any point in going there after that because the evacuation would be continued on the 13th, but that is the number of citizens who happened to be at the DutchBat base. So there was no need for me to go up there anymore.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, let's focus a little bit on the 14th of July 1995. Do you remember whether or not you had any meetings with Mr. Deronjic on the 14th of July 1995?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: I don't recall that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Do you remember having any meetings with Davidovic on the 14th of July 1995?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: I had no need to have any meetings with Mr. Davidovic. He knows what his work is, I know what is mine, and there was no need for me to have a meeting in order to, I don't know, do what at that meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Well, did you see him at all on the 14th of July 1995?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: I don't remember. I probably saw him. He is just across the hall from my office, or his office is just across from mine. I don't remember. I don't actually have any associations with anything else regarding if I saw him or not. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. Help me with this, and then we are going to get is to some concrete issues relating to your testimony in the Blagojevic case. But when did you first learn of the execution or the killing of the Bosnian Muslim in the Kravica warehouse? Was Mr. Davidovic told you that on the morning of the 13th in the morning when you stated that you came late for work, is that when you first learned of it?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: Davidovic didn't tell me that --

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Right. When was that --

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: But actually Nikolic told me, meaning that probably the next morning, I don't know if this happened the day before or not, I'm not sure now, but I'm sure that Nikolic came in the morning and said that this happened. It probably happened the day before. I don't know at what time.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. So --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, Mr. Ostojic, Mr. Gosnell.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Mr. President, I have to object to the last question, albeit belatedly. Not only does it misstate what he said here today, it misstates what he said in Blagojevic, and I'm not sure how my learned friend could have misunderstood what was previously said.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: We'll clarify it for the record, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead. Thank you, Mr. Gosnell.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Is it your testimony, Mr. Simic, that you never discussed the Kravica warehouse killings with Mr. Davidovic?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And is it likewise your testimony that you never discussed the Kravica warehouse killings with Mr. Deronjic?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And you were informed of this massacre by only one individual Jovan Nikolic; and can you tell us what, if any, action you took to find more information about the circumstances of the Kravica warehouse massacre once you learned of that information?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: I don't have any authority to be able to take such steps, and I said the same thing the last time. This was a combat zone, that area is under the control of the army and the police, I don't know what I would have done if I had happened to be there with a vehicle and a man in civilian clothes. I probably could have talked about it with Deronjic later and asked him if he had been informed enough and could something like this could have been avoided and did things have to go exactly the way they went. But this happened much later after the event.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Gosnell.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Simic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Mr. President, there's a word missing at page 29, line 11.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Under the control of the.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: He said army and the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: I do agree, and I thought it was important for that to be on the record now. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Simic, I'm not asking you what you thought your obligations were at that time given your duties and capacity in that town of Bratunac what to do once you learned that information, I'm simply asking you what you actually did. Am I correct in understanding that you did nothing once you learned that information?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know to this day what I could have done. I mean, I don't know, are you asking me -- I don't know what I could have done on that day from the office.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I just want to know --

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: I mean, if you have any suggestions, I would like to hear them.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: We can discuss that at another time. I'm trying to find out what actually did you, sir, you did nothing once you learned that information; correct?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: I was horrified when I heard that. That's all that I could do.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, let me ask you this, sir, with respect to this issue that appears on page 7626 of your Blagojevic testimony on the 15th of April 2004, you discuss learning of convoys carrying people to Bratunac. Do you remember that general topic?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: I didn't understand the question completely. Can you be a little bit more specific, what convoy?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Fair enough. Convoy with Bosnian-Muslim men that apparently was brought to Bratunac, according to you in your testimony at page 7626, you state that you had this conversation, I think, with Mr. Davidovic, and you were informed that overnight a convoy of Bosnian-Muslims was brought to Bratunac. Are you familiar with that issue or topic?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes, I am. And I said what I had to say about that topic. Maybe you can put the specific question now. What --

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you for that direction. That happened on the 13th of July 1995, and that was the time that you claim that you came late to work and had this meeting with Davidovic; correct?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, at any time prior to that, were there any Bosnian-Muslim POWs in Bratunac, meaning on the 12th or the 11th of July?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, there weren't. And last time I tried to present the sequence of my movements that day and what I was able to see from the route of my movement of that day, and I described it in as much detail as I was able to, as much as my memory serves me about past events. But I think I did state the most important things the way that it happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And we have that, thank you. Now, the next thing that occurs, did you say that that convoy, sir, left after you did some inquiring, that that convoy actually left that same day or the people who were brought to Bratunac left that same day, to Tuzla or Kladanj; correct?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: So --

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: The president of the executive board informed me about that. He said that they had gone and that we can breathe a sigh of relief after that, and that problem doesn't exist anymore, I talked about that and I don't think there's any need to repeat it.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I appreciate your thoughts on that, but tell me this: Did all the Bosnian-Muslims that were brought to Bratunac on the 13th, meaning on the evening of the 12th and that were in Bratunac on the 13th of July, when did they leave Bratunac, did they leave actually on the 13th in the afternoon, in the evening, or did they leave sometime thereafter?

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Gosnell. One moment, sir. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: The manner of asking that question was improper. It clearly pushes the witness towards an answer that is -- may I ask the witness to take his earphones off.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Simic, do you understand English? Do you not understand English?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Can you remove your headphones for awhile, please. Yes, Mr. Gosnell.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Of course my learned friend is entitled to ask leading questions but leading questions which egregiously at variance with what he said in his testimony I think may in certain circumstances be improper, and this is one such circumstance. He is pushing him towards an answer that is at variance with his testimony and doesn't give him an opportunity to give an answer that's consistent with his previous testimony, so I just wish to place that objection on the record, Your Honour and perhaps ask my friend to restate his question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You have a remedy on redirect if you want. If you want to. And secondly, Mr. Ostojic, having heard you as a gentleman enough now to adjust his question and give the opportunity to the witness if he needs to change anything or explain anything. Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Just to add something to that objection, I don't think there's a problem pushing the witness to go somewhere, but the previous question suggested that this witness had said they had left on the 13th, which is not correct, and so he can't misstate the record. But it wasn't exactly clear what date he was talking about, so I think that last question may have hopefully cleared it up, so that's just my --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you, again even you will have the opportunity to go through any terrain that has been left uncleared. Yes, Mr. Ostojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I appreciate both my learned friends to follow the transcript and listen to the testimony because the witness did say that they left. And my friend from the Prosecution, he can look at that specific page and line number, and I will clarify it. I think if my learned friend from the Defence just looks at page 7627 specifically line 14 of that transcript, he will know that his answer with respect to specifically when that convoy left was not only ambiguous, although I wouldn't all egregious on how he may have answered it or coined it. I think it's necessary for this Trial Chamber to hear when this individual given his capacity knows or thinks he believes that convoy or those Bosnian Muslims from Bratunac left. But I will, Mr. President, with your leave inquire further so we can flush this out a little bit. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Simic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Simic, I'd like you to help us a little bit because we are a little confused with respect to the Bosnian-Muslims and this convoy that arrived in Bratunac in July -- on or about July 12th or 13th 1995. We know, I think, and it's pretty clear that you learned of this for the first time on the morning or late morning of the 13th of July 1995. Can you give us first, before I ask you when these Bosnian-Muslims left, how many were there approximately, do you know? Did you discuss that with anyone?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: A little more specificity, women and children or men, because in this context this question could be several things.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Fair enough. I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Fair enough.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead. You need to explain the difference.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I will.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Simic, we are still on the topic of the convoy or convoys that were brought to Bratunac overnight according to your testimony. Do you know what the makeup of the people within those convoys was?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: I don't know, but the president of the executive board went to them, he alerted the Red Cross to provide food for those people because according to his information those people spent the night at the stadium, it was a horrible piece of news a horrible thing that had happened at all. It was a like a time bomb for the whole town, I'm not going to go into explanations about why this was dangerous for the town, and the president of the executive board was there, he saw it, I did not. I didn't. He said there was a large number of buses, I don't know how many, that is, I don't know if this is ten, five, exactly how many are many. And the fact that even two or three buses were brought to the stadium and put in the situation that they were in, that was horrible in itself. I didn't go into any more details. He was very frightened about that and he asked me to urgently --

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So you don't know. That's really your basic answer, you don't know whether they were men, women, or children that were brought to Bratunac according to you on the evening of the 12th of July 1995?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: I think that he said that they were men, that was men. That is the point, the whole point why we were afraid, why men were left in buses to spend the rest of the night and they were still there when I got there because no one from the responsible army people appeared to resolve this question. And there could have been an incident at any moment and as time went on the incident could have been more immediate and that is why we were justifiably afraid.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Simic. We have that already in your transcript actually from the Blagojevic case, but thank you for that again. What I'd like to know now is, when, if at all, when, if at all, did those men or those people who were brought to Bratunac, when did they leave, or did they ever leave?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: They definitely left. Let's be most global without specifying. I'm not in a position to be able to do that, but definitely in the early morning hours, we were in a hurry, it was hot, both of us experienced this heat the day before, and we knew how it would be for those people in Bratunac in the sun, in the bus. It was a very hot summer.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: So it still didn't really clarify it I don't think. Early morning hours that same day when you came late to work or the next day, sir, did they get evacuated? So help me with this, walk through it with me. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: Immediately after my conversation with Davidovic, I intervened and there was a promise made that the convoy would leave immediately and Mr. Davidovic told me that the convoy had left.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: That's what I wanted to clarify, thank you for that, sir. After that group of convoys or Bosnian-Muslims left, that means on the 13th of July 1995, did Bratunac have any further Bosnian-Muslims men, children, or women who were brought to Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: I didn't have any information about that, and I was not in a position to see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Do you know or are you familiar with the school the Vuk Karadzic school?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And do you know if any Bosnian-Muslims were held in the Vuk Karadzic school from the period of the 12th to the 15th of July 1995?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: At the time when this was happening and in the days after that, I didn't know that. But I did hear later that this did happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. And before we break, sir, we have a couple of minutes, I'd like to talk to awe little bit more about your testimony in the Blagojevic case, the 15th of April 2004. You were called as a Defence witness for Mr. Blagojevic; correct?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And at that time, July 1995, Blagojevic held the position of commander of the Bratunac Brigade; correct?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, during that time period in July of 1995, had you seen Mr. Blagojevic in Bratunac at all?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: I saw that and -- actually, I saw him and in my previous testimony I described where I saw him and what my recollection is of how Mr. Blagojevic looked then when I saw him, because even to this day I remember that and I can describe it now if necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: We have it, thank you. What I'd like to know is how many times prior to your testimony for Mr. Blagojevic did you meet with the attorneys for Mr. Blagojevic?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: Twice.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And did you meet with them ever in Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: Once in Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And the other time would be where, in The Hague?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: In The Hague, when he came to testify in briefings, I think that's what it is called.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Did you, sir, at any time keep any notes or diary?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Proofing, interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Did you, sir, keep any notes or diaries of the meetings that you had either in July 1995 or with attorneys in preparation for your testimony in trials?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: No, I never did anything like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: It's my understanding, sir, that you also testified in two other cases, one last year in July of 2007 in the Bosnian court; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And also, sir, you testified in another case in the Bosnian-Sarajevo court in January of 2008 this year; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: It's correct that I testified twice. I'm not sure about the dates. I think you are right. I'm sure you have the dates as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: We have the transcripts actually, we'll go over them a little bit after the break. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I think it might be time, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. We'll have a 25 minute break now, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: --- Resumed at 11.00 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ostojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Simic, if we can --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: If we can continue here, sir, in July 1995, to the best of your recollection, do you know if Mr. Deronjic was appointed to any position, such as civil commissioner?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: I heard that he had been appointed from the president. Now, I don't know about his duties. I think it mostly had to do with his exercising control over the civilian population, the situation among the civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: The civilians that you have in mind are the Muslims; correct?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And when was he appointed to that position?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: Well, I was not there. I may have heard it over the radio or perhaps the president of the executive board told me. That's immaterial. But I heard about it. It may have been the 11th, the 10th, something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And just so we are clear, sir, the 11th and 10th of July 1995; correct?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: I don't know the exact date when he was appointed, but he was appointed in the Srebrenica case.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. Well, I'm just following up on your answer, sir, which appears on page 39 line 12 where you say "the 11th, the 10th, something like that." Whatever date it was it was in July of 1995; correct?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: When you say "president," because I know there's a lot of presidents that float around in Bratunac from the executive economy to the SDS, but the president you are refer together is Radovan Karadzic, correct? That's who appointed Deronjic.

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes, definitely. I didn't have any authority to make such a decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I'm not suggesting that you did. I just want toed clarify which president you were refer together. I thought it was pretty obvious, but thank you for that. I wanted to bring up to e-court Exhibit 1149 A and B, which is an intercept. Sir, on the screen you'll have an opportunity to see this intercept. As it's being brought up on e-court, have you at any time with the lawyers from Blagojevic or in this case had an opportunity to review any intercepts?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Also 115 B, I am sorry. We are going to show you an intercept. We have the English version up, in a second or two we'll have the B/C/S version up. This purports to be a intercept on the second half of that page of a conversation between Mr. Deronjic and president Karadzic and his intermediary, just so you are clear, you'll see some dots there. And it seems as if, and I think we are all in relative agreement on this, it seems to suggest that Dr. Karadzic was conveying something to a person sitting next to him and he was conveying it to Mr. Deronjic. And it really goes to the issue that we were discussing prior to the break, and that's the issue of the Bosnian-Muslims coming into Bratunac on or about the 12th or so of July. This intercept however, according to the Prosecution, I believe, is dated the 13th of July 1995, and I wanted to know if you have any information about this. So be kind enough to read the second portion of that page on B/C/S, 1149B, and if you need, we can enlarge that?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: Well, could you please zoom in a little bit because I haven't been able to read anything from the start at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I have a copy, if the Court thinks perhaps -- it's now been enlarged.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, the important thing is the B/C/S version is under seal, so we have already given instructions while you were.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So let's proceed with caution.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Fair enough.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Yes. It's my understanding, sir, we just won't mention who the people were who purportedly captured this conversation, but we can talk about the contents of the conversation. So let me know when you've had an opportunity to review this.

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes, I've read this part now.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: The designation D is for Deronjic, as you can see, what I wants to focus on is in the middle portion of this intercept Deronjic seems to say, as they discuss how many thousands, he says, "... but there will be more during the night." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now if this conversation happened on the 13th of July 1995, given your testimony under oath here earlier this morning that there were no such prisoners or Bosnian-Muslims in Bratunac after they were evacuated, what is Deronjic talking about, to the best of your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: I really cannot fathom what Deronjic is saying here.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: This conversation is timed at 2010 hours, do you see that? It's right on the top on the right-hand first line?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I can see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Then as you read through the intercept, it seems to be, am I correct that Karadzic is instructing Deronjic as to what to do with what he calls "all the goods must be placed inside the warehouses before 12.00 tomorrow." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Do you know what that is in reference to?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And then further it seems that president Karadzic through his intermediary says, "Deronjic not in the warehouses, and then a word that is not legible, over there, but somewhere else." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Do you know anything about that, what are they referencing, where do they want the goods or the thousands of --

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: I have no idea.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, one moment. Yes, Mr. Gosnell.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Mr. President, the witness has now answered twice that he doesn't know about the nature of this conversation or the contents thereof.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. You are right. He hasn't got a clue as to what Deronjic is talking about. That's what he has said.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I heard that for that first portion, I now heard it for the second portion. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Simic, at any time subsequent to July of 1995, did you discuss with Mr. Deronjic at all who was responsible for the thousands of Bosnian-Muslims and where they were transferred in the warehouse or who gave them any instruction that they should be transferred from Bratunac to another area? Did you ever discuss that with Deronjic?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Are you, sir, familiar with the fact, or is it known to you that Deronjic had a meeting with President Karadzic on the 14th of July 1995?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: 1995, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Let's bring up Exhibit P2905 quickly. And it's really the second portion, second part of that exhibit as well, which is the lower bottom. If you look at the fourth entry, I believe, which has a plus sign, 1100 hours, do you see that, sir?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And we do have an English translation that I think has been provided to the court, but it still may be in draft from my understanding they are work on the rest of the diary. Do you see the entry for Miroslav Deronjic and that he met with President Karadzic for a half an hour and then subsequent to that, he had a 4-hour meeting with the delegation from Srebrenica. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: I don't know anything about meeting either.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. He has answered the question. I think it's -- but still, if you want to give.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Your Honour, same objection as before, the witness indicated he doesn't have any knowledge of this and then we have --

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Were you part of the delegation, sir?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: Never. I was never a member of any delegation that included Deronjic at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, let me turn, sir --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Simic, I take it that Mr. Deronjic -- Davidovic and you are the individuals who took up the very sort of important position in Bratunac, is it fair to say so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, you could say that. I was the president of the assembly and Davidovic was the president of the executive board, and Deronjic was the president of the party, and he was given this power by the president, and I never saw this in writing. And in fact, I didn't even inquire that much about what Deronjic was given because that was his problem, not mine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The document you are seeing in front of you is a memo written by Mira allegedly a secretary of Dr. Karadzic, and we have evidence to the effect that Mr. Deronjic met individually with Dr. Karadzic for half an hour and later on for hour hours with the delegation from Srebrenica. So one may assume that in that delegation, such important persons like Davidovic or yourself might have been included. What would you say to that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There's no foundation for that at all. It's completely groundless because we never attended any such meeting, the task that Deronjic was given, he was given by the president, and it had nothing to do with me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Or you might have heard anything with respect to this meeting with Dr. Karadzic from Deronjic who was your friend?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Nobody told us about that, and I didn't have time to talk about it. Well, I can now explain to you at length why that was the case. You could see that this was a logical sequence of events and that in principle I didn't want to interfere with anyone's business, at the same time I didn't allow anyone to interfere in my business.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ostojic. Sorry to interrupt you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: If I may follow up on this a little bit. Sir, you know that Mr. Deronjic pled guilty to acts and events that occurred in Bratunac in approximately 1992, 1993; correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't know how much that is correct, Mr. Ostojic, because Deronjic, I sat on that case. I sat on that case. He pled guilty to the events in Glogova in May of 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Fair enough, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It was a very limited indictment, very specific event in which 64 or 84 persons were allegedly killed. Were killed actually because he pled guilty to it. Had nothing to do with Bratunac as such.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I'll clarify that, I didn't mean to mislead the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, how far is Glogova from Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know exactly. Maybe 4 or 5 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: You grew up in Bratunac, you've lived there, you teach there, you went to school there, and you are familiar obviously with the fact that Deronjic pled guilty to crimes that is occurred in Glogova, 5 kilometres or less from Bratunac, are you not?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: The Bosnian-Muslim men that were massacred in Kravica in July of 1995, you are also familiar that they were buried in Glogova, were they not?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And do you know what role, if any, Mr. Mrkovic Dragan had in connection with the burial of those Bosnian-Muslim men?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: No, because Mrkovic was not my subordinate, he could have been the subordinate of the president of the executive board.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Davidovic -- was it Davidovic that he was subordinate to?
